newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks seen in range-bound.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks seen in range-bound.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market's key Nikkei index is likely to slip into range-bound trade during the coming week as investors tread warily ahead of month's end, brokers said.
"We probably won't see further buying from institutional investors next week as the end of the month is approaching," said Masaaki Higashida, strategist at Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
Higashida expected the Nikkei average to hover between 20,500 and 21,500.
On Friday, the key Nikkei 225 average closed at 21,216.11, up 286.38 points from its closing on November 15.

Most investors are expected to keep a low profile ahead of the Bank of Japan's "tankan" survey of business sentiment due out on Wednesday, which will indicate the state of the current economic recovery, brokers said.
"If the outcome of the survey is rosy, it may prompt some funds to shift to stocks from bonds," said Kaoru Ichikawa, a senior trader at Kokusai Securities Co Ltd.
He also said he would focus on how a string of Japanese bank earnings results, which were released on Friday, would affect shares in the banking sector.
Some analysts said there were some external factors the market had yet to consider.
"We don't yet know how the recent political scandals and abolition of the special tax cuts will move the market," said Keiji Arai, strategist at Sanyo Securities Co Ltd.

On Thursday, Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa told a news conference that Japanese special income-tax cuts, which were aimed at stimulating the economy, should be stopped from next fiscal year, because the economic recovery is now more solid.

Also on Thursday, a Japanese newspaper reported that two political fund-raising groups supporting Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto received cash totalling 4.5 million yen ($40,450) from groups indirectly linked to a company run by an executive at the centre of a health-care bribery scandal.
The two political groups donated a total of 76 million yen to a dozen politicians, including Hashimoto, the paper said.
